messages.subject: Change matrix dimension
parts:
Hello,
I was wondering how to change a matrix dimension in the nimbleCode.

For exemple I have a matrice matrix of dimension 500 8 that I want to transform into a vector of dimension 4000, then turn it back into a matrix

I tried with:
- unlist(matrix) but it is nor working in Nimble code
- dim(matrix) <- c(4000,1) and reversly dim(vector)<-c(500,8) also not working
- nimDim(matrix)<-c(4000,1) and reversly dim(vector)<-c(500,8) but apparently nimDim do not support to be changed (contrary to dim out of Nimble script)

As I explained, I need it in both ways: from a matrix to one vector, and then from one vector to a matrix.
For the first part I did it with a for loop and I may be able to do it like that also for the second part but I was wondering if there was a simplier way.

Thank you in adavnce

Ugoline

messages.author: bebd85531a67ef86
messages.subject: Re: Change matrix dimension
parts:
There is the setSize function. To quote the manual "Its purpose is to explicitly resize a multivariate object (vector, matrix or array), currently up to 4 dimensions."  This is particularly important if you are compiling the code to C++.

But in the example you give, it is unclear if you really need setSize, or if you could just get by with creating new multivariate objects.

I hope that helps
David

messages.author: c9e9cbbfb3b043f0
messages.subject: Re: Change matrix dimension
parts:
Short answer for Ugoline, in NIMBLE, numeric objects (scalars, vectors, matricies, 3d-arrays, etc) must always remain the same dimension.  That is, a vector a length [anything] can be resized to have a different length, but that particular variable must and will always remain a (1d) vector.  Similarly, a (2d) matrix can be resized to have a different number of columns or rows, but will always be a matrix.

One note of caution.  If you have a 3x3 matrix X, for example, containing the numbers 1...9, then you resize it to be a 10x10 matrix..... then the elements of X[1:3, 1:3] will generally *not* still contain the numbers 1...9 as they were before.  That is, resizing does *not* generally preserve the existing contents of matrices, arrays, etc.

There is the setSize function. To quote the manual "Its purpose is to explicitly resize a multivariate object (vector, matrix or array), currently up to 4 dimensions."  This is particularly important if you are compiling the code to C++.

But in the example you give, it is unclear if you really need setSize, or if you could just get by with creating new multivariate objects.

I hope that helps
David

messages.author: 0ef2647ddd7095d7
messages.subject: Re: Change matrix dimension
parts:
Thanks David and Daniel.

Daniel, for a while now setSize has taken an argument “copy” that defaults to TRUE.  I think you are recalling that an early version of setSize did not guarantee contents are preserved, but now it does.  If contents do not need to be preserved, one can use copy=FALSE and possibly gain some performance.  help(setSize) covers this.

One can convert from vectors to matrices and vice-versa in several ways, although they must be different variables.  I hope the following example is useful:

library(nimble)

foo <- nimbleFunction(
    run = function(m = double(2)) {
        v <- numeric(length(m), value = m) ## convert matrix to vector 
        print("v = ", v)
        m <- matrix(v, nrow = 4) ## assign vector into matrix
        print("m = ", m)
        newDims <- c(2, 5) 
        setSize(m, newDims) ## resize matrix
        print("m = ", m)
        setSize(m, 5, 2) ## another way to resize matrix
        print("m = ", m)
    })

cfoo <- compileNimble(foo)

m <- matrix(1:20, nrow = 2)
foo(m)
cfoo(m) ## note that C++ matrix output from “print" looks different, but results are the same

-Perry

One note of caution.  If you have a 3x3 matrix X, for example, containing the numbers 1...9, then you resize it to be a 10x10 matrix..... then the elements of X[1:3, 1:3] will generally *not* still contain the numbers 1...9 as they were before.  That is, resizing does *not* generally preserve the existing contents of matrices, arrays, etc.
